title: Cold-shock protocol to bleach Aiptasia
author: Pringle lab
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.qx8dxrw
materials: Chill a large volume of seawater to 4°C.

steps.title: Prepare anemone tank
steps.instruction: Set up a tank containing Aiptasia anemones; it is preferable (but not required) to let them sit until they adhere to the sides or bottom of the tank.

steps.title: Cold‑shock water exchange
steps.instruction: Pour out the existing seawater from the tank and replace it with seawater chilled to 4 °C. Place the entire tank in a 4 °C refrigerator or cold room.

steps.title: Incubate at 4 °C
steps.instruction: Incubate the tank at 4 °C for exactly 4 hours (04:00:00).

steps.title: Return to room temperature
steps.instruction: Remove the tank from the 4 °C environment, pour out the cold water, and replace it with seawater at room temperature. The anemones will expel algal boluses that appear as dark brown balls.

steps.title: Repeat water changes
steps.instruction: Perform 2–3 additional water changes by pouring out the tank water and refilling with room‑temperature seawater each time.

steps.title: Dark recovery period
steps.instruction: Place the tank in complete darkness (e.g., a dark cabinet) at room temperature for 1–2 days. Replace the seawater with fresh room‑temperature seawater once per day.

steps.title: Choose bleaching method
steps.instruction: Decide whether to use the faster, harsher method or the slower, gentler method for DCMU bleaching.

steps.title: Prepare DCMU seawater
steps.instruction: Make seawater containing DCMU (or diuron, 3‑[3,4‑dichlorophenyl]‑1,1‑dimethylurea) at a final concentration of 10 µM–50 µM. Higher concentrations act faster but are harsher, possibly requiring more frequent water changes.

steps.title: Fast bleaching – dark maintenance
steps.instruction: Leave the tank in complete darkness with regular room‑temperature seawater. Change the water every 1–2 days. Feed the anemones at least once a week (preferably 2–3 times per week). Whenever feeding occurs, change the water the following day.

steps.title: Fast bleaching – DCMU treatment
steps.instruction: Remove the tank from the dark cabinet, replace the seawater with the prepared DCMU‑seawater, and incubate at room temperature under constant light for several weeks.

substeps.instruction: Replace the DCMU‑seawater once or twice per week, adjusting frequency if the anemones appear stressed.
Feed brine shrimp at least once per week (2–3 times per week is better). After each feeding, change the water the next day.

steps.title: Fast bleaching – screening for algae
steps.instruction: After 2–3 weeks of DCMU treatment, examine the anemones under a fluorescence stereoscope to assess the presence of residual algae. Continue DCMU incubation until the anemones appear aposymbiotic. Refer to the guidelines section for appropriate fluorescence filter settings.

steps.title: Slow bleaching – extended dark maintenance
steps.instruction: If the slower method is chosen, keep the tank in complete darkness with regular room‑temperature seawater, changing water every 1–2 days and feeding as described above. Continue this dark incubation for up to 1.5 months before screening.

steps.title: Slow bleaching – DCMU treatment
steps.instruction: After the extended dark period, replace the seawater with DCMU‑seawater (10 µM–50 µM) and incubate at room temperature under constant light, following the same water‑change and feeding schedule as in the fast method.

steps.title: Slow bleaching – screening for algae
steps.instruction: After approximately 1.5 months of DCMU treatment, screen the anemones under a fluorescence stereoscope for algal presence. Continue incubation in the dark until the anemones appear aposymbiotic.

steps.title: Confirm aposymbiosis
steps.instruction: When anemones appear aposymbiotic, transfer a subset to room‑temperature seawater under light (without DCMU) and incubate for 1 week. After the week, check for algae under a fluorescence stereoscope. If any algae are detected, resume DCMU treatment; if none are detected, the anemones are fully aposymbiotic.
